hypotheses.title: SushiRouterSmol hardcodes 1e18 output, ignoring real swap amounts
hypotheses.description: `swapExactTokensForETH` and `swapExactETHForTokens` both use a hardcoded `one = 1 * 10 ** 18` as the swap amount, ignoring `amountIn` and `msg.value` entirely. `swapExactTokensForETH` pulls `amountIn` from the caller but only withdraws and sends `one` (1e18) of WETH to `to`; the rest of the pulled tokens are retained by the router. `swapExactETHForTokens` deposits only `one` of `msg.value` into WETH and sends `one` of the output token, retaining the rest of the ETH. Any caller using this router loses the difference between the actual amount and 1e18.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (or any user) calls `swapExactTokensForETH` with `amountIn = 100e18`. 2) Router pulls 100e18 tokens from the caller, but only sends 1e18 worth of ETH to `to`. 3) The remaining 99e18 tokens are stuck in the router (recoverable only by whoever can call `rescueFunds`-like logic, which this contract lacks). 4) Similarly for `swapExactETHForTokens`, the excess ETH is trapped.
hypotheses.impact: Direct loss of user funds: the difference between the requested amount and 1e18 is permanently trapped in the router, and the user receives far less than expected.
hypotheses.recommendation: Replace the hardcoded `one` with the actual `amountIn` (for token→ETH) and `msg.value` (for ETH→token), and use the real path amounts.

hypotheses.title: ETH_RUNE.transferTo uses tx.origin enabling phishing theft
hypotheses.description: transferTo() transfers tokens from `tx.origin` to an arbitrary recipient without any approval. Any contract that a user interacts with can call transferTo() on the user's behalf, moving the user's ETH.RUNE to an attacker-controlled address. This is a classic tx.origin phishing vector.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a malicious contract. 2) Victim calls a function on the malicious contract (e.g., a fake swap). 3) The malicious contract calls ETH_RUNE.transferTo(attacker, victimBalance), which transfers the victim's tokens to the attacker.
hypotheses.impact: Complete theft of victim ETH.RUNE balances.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove transferTo or replace tx.origin with msg.sender and require explicit approval.

hypotheses.title: SushiRouterSmol uses hardcoded "one" instead of actual amountIn
hypotheses.description: The function ignores `amountIn` for pricing and instead uses a hardcoded `one = 1e18` value for `amounts`. The user's real `amountIn` is pulled via `safeTransferFrom` but the output amount is always computed as 1e18 (and WETH withdrawn as 1e18). This breaks the swap economics: the min-out check compares against a constant, not the real swap output.
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted caller invokes `swapExactTokensForETH` with a manipulated `amountOutMin` close to 1e18 and any `amountIn` (e.g., tiny dust). The contract pulls the full `amountIn` from the caller, withdraws 1e18 WETH from the pool contract, and sends 1e18 ETH to `to`. Since `amountOutMin` only needs to be <= 1e18, the attacker can extract 1e18 WETH/ETH from the router's WETH balance by supplying only dust tokens.
hypotheses.impact: Complete drainage of WETH reserves held by the router; the caller receives far more ETH than the tokens they supplied justify. Loss of funds in the router/aggregator.
hypotheses.recommendation: Replace the hardcoded `[one]` array with the correct UniswapV2 path amounts derived from `amountIn` and reserves, or remove this stub and call the real Sushi router.

hypotheses.title: Anyone can drain vault allowances via transferOut with zero allowance
hypotheses.description: transferOut() has no access control and uses msg.sender as the vault whose allowance is debited. Any external caller can invoke it with an arbitrary `to` and `asset`, and the function will decrement `_vaultAllowance[msg.sender][asset]` and transfer tokens held by the router to `to`. Since the router holds all deposited ARC-20 tokens, an attacker who has any nonzero allowance (or who can trigger underflow-free paths) can move router-held tokens to themselves.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls deposit() with a tiny amount of an ARC-20 to credit `_vaultAllowance[attacker][asset]`. 2) Attacker calls transferOut(attacker, asset, amount, "") — the router transfers its held tokens to the attacker. 3) Repeat for any asset the router holds.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of all ARC-20 tokens custodied by the router; loss of user deposits.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict transferOut/transferOutAndCall/returnVaultAssets to registered vaults via an allowlist or signature check.

hypotheses.title: THORChain_Router._transferOutAndCallV5 ignores swapOutV5 failure for ERC20
hypotheses.description: In the ERC20 branch, the router transfers the ERC20 to the aggregator and then calls `swapOutV5` via a low-level call, but the boolean `_dexAggSuccess` is never checked. If the aggregator fails (reverts or returns false), the router still emits `TransferOutAndCallV5` as if the swap succeeded. The ERC20 has already been sent to the aggregator, so the funds are stuck or lost.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a malicious aggregator that accepts the ERC20 transfer but reverts in `swapOutV5`. 2) Attacker triggers `transferOutAndCallV5` with `fromAsset` = victim token and `target` = malicious aggregator. 3) The router transfers the ERC20 to the aggregator and calls `swapOutV5`, which reverts. 4) The router ignores the failure and emits a success event. 5) The aggregator keeps the ERC20.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of vault ERC20 funds; Bifrost observes a successful outbound transfer while the user receives nothing.
hypotheses.recommendation: Check `_dexAggSuccess` and revert (or handle the failure by returning the ERC20 to the vault) if the aggregator call fails.

hypotheses.title: transferAllowance lets anyone move allowances between arbitrary vaults
hypotheses.description: transferAllowance() is external with no caller restriction. When `router == address(this)`, it calls `_adjustAllowances(newVault, asset, amount)` which debits `_vaultAllowance[msg.sender][asset]` and credits `_vaultAllowance[newVault][asset]`. Any untrusted caller can therefore move allowance credit from any vault they can impersonate (their own) to an arbitrary newVault, or, combined with transferOut, redirect funds.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deposits a small amount to get a nonzero allowance. 2) Attacker calls transferAllowance(address(this), attackerControlledVault, asset, amount, "") to shift credit. 3) Attacker then calls transferOut from the credited vault to drain router-held tokens.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized movement of vault allowances and theft of router-custodied assets.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require msg.sender to be a registered vault (allowlist) before allowing allowance adjustments.

hypotheses.title: returnVaultAssets callable by anyone to redirect vault assets
hypotheses.description: returnVaultAssets() is external with no access control. When `router == address(this)`, it calls `_adjustAllowances(asgard, coins[i].asset, coins[i].amount)` for each coin, debiting `_vaultAllowance[msg.sender][asset]` and crediting `asgard`. An attacker can pass an `asgard` they control and arbitrary coin amounts to move allowance credit to themselves, then call transferOut to drain the router.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains a small allowance via deposit(). 2) Attacker calls returnVaultAssets(address(this), attackerAddr, coins, "") with coins matching router-held assets. 3) Attacker calls transferOut(attacker, asset, amount, "") to withdraw the credited allowance.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of all router-custodied ARC-20/ERC-20 tokens.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict returnVaultAssets to registered vaults only.

hypotheses.title: THORChain_Router._transferOutAndCallV5 sends ETH to target on swap failure
hypotheses.description: In the ETH branch, if `swapOutV5` fails, the router attempts to send `msg.value` to `aggregationPayload.target` (the aggregator) instead of to the intended recipient. The comment says "just send the recipient the gas asset" but the code sends to `target`. If the target is a contract that accepts ETH, the funds are lost to the aggregator.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a malicious aggregator that reverts in `swapOutV5` but has a payable fallback. 2) Attacker triggers `transferOutAndCallV5` with `fromAsset` = address(0) and `target` = malicious aggregator. 3) The router calls `swapOutV5`, which reverts. 4) The router sends `msg.value` to the malicious aggregator via `send`. 5) The aggregator keeps the ETH.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of vault ETH to a malicious aggregator; user receives nothing.
hypotheses.recommendation: Send the fallback ETH to `aggregationPayload.recipient` (or back to `msg.sender`), not to `target`.

hypotheses.title: transferOutAndCallV5 ERC20 path ignores swap failure and leaves tokens stuck
hypotheses.description: In the ERC20 branch, the router decrements `_vaultAllowance[msg.sender][fromAsset] -= fromAmount`, transfers `fromAmount` to the aggregator target, then calls `swapOutV5` on the target. The return value `_dexAggSuccess` is deliberately ignored (comment says "if the aggregator fails, the transaction should not revert"). If the aggregator reverts, the tokens remain at the aggregator contract, but the vault's allowance has already been debited and the `TransferOutAndCallV5` event is emitted as if the swap succeeded. The vault's accounting now shows the tokens as spent while they are actually held by an arbitrary aggregator.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (any vault caller, or a malicious aggregator whitelisted by fuzzy-match) triggers `transferOutAndCallV5` with an ERC20 `fromAsset`. 2) The aggregator's `swapOutV5` reverts (e.g., malicious aggregator always reverts). 3) Router still debits the vault allowance and emits success event. 4) Tokens sit at the aggregator; the vault's on-chain allowance no longer reflects them.
hypotheses.impact: Vault allowance is debited while tokens are stranded at the aggregator; the vault's real holdings and its recorded allowance diverge, and the aggregator can later sweep the tokens via `rescueFunds` (owner) or its own logic.
hypotheses.recommendation: Either revert on aggregator failure, or return the tokens to the router/vault and only debit the allowance on success; at minimum, do not emit a success event when the swap failed.

hypotheses.title: THORChain_Aggregator.swapIn approves swapRouter with `amount` not `_safeAmount`
hypotheses.description: `swapIn` computes `_safeAmount` as the actual received amount (accounting for fee-on-transfer tokens) but then calls `safeApprove(token, address(swapRouter), amount)` using the original `amount` parameter. If the token charges a transfer fee, the aggregator approves more than it holds, and the subsequent `swapExactTokensForETH` will revert or the swap will fail. Conversely, if the token is deflationary, the approval exceeds the balance.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker uses a fee-on-transfer token as `token`. 2) Attacker calls `swapIn` with `amount` larger than the actual received `_safeAmount`. 3) The aggregator approves `amount` to the swap router but only holds `_safeAmount`. 4) The swap router's `transferFrom` fails or the swap reverts, locking the user's tokens in the aggregator.
hypotheses.impact: User funds stuck in the aggregator; swapIn is unusable for fee-on-transfer tokens.
hypotheses.recommendation: Approve `_safeAmount` instead of `amount`.

hypotheses.title: transferOutAndCallV5 forwards arbitrary payload to untrusted target without validation
hypotheses.description: The V5 aggregator path takes a fully attacker-controlled TransferOutAndCallData struct (target, fromAsset, fromAmount, toAsset, recipient, amountOutMin, payload, originAddress) and performs a low-level call to target with the encoded swapOutV5 selector. There is no whitelist check, no signature over the payload, and no binding to the originating vault's intent. Any caller can supply an arbitrary target contract and arbitrary payload, and the router will forward value/ERC20 to it. The only "authentication" is that msg.sender must have a vault allowance, but the allowance is decremented by fromAmount which the attacker also controls.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains a small vault allowance (or is a vault). 2) Attacker calls transferOutAndCallV5 with target = attacker-controlled contract, fromAsset = address(0), fromAmount = 0, payload = malicious calldata. 3) Router forwards msg.value to attacker contract and emits TransferOutAndCallV5 with attacker-chosen originAddress. 4) Bifrost may interpret the event as a legitimate outbound swap.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of router-held ETH/ERC20 via arbitrary call, spoofed originAddress in events leading to incorrect Bifrost accounting, potential draining of vault allowances.
hypotheses.recommendation: Whitelist aggregator targets, require an EIP-712 signature over the full payload from the vault, and bind originAddress to the actual msg.sender.

hypotheses.title: AvaxAggregator.swapIn approves swapRouter with `amount` not `safeAmount`
hypotheses.description: `swapIn` computes `safeAmount` as the actual received amount after `safeTransferFrom`, but then calls `IERC20(token).safeApprove(address(swapRouter), amount)` using the original `amount` parameter. For fee-on-transfer tokens, the approval exceeds the aggregator's balance, causing the subsequent `swapExactTokensForAVAX` to revert or fail.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker uses a fee-on-transfer token as `token`. 2) Attacker calls `swapIn` with `amount` larger than the actual received `safeAmount`. 3) The aggregator approves `amount` to the swap router but only holds `safeAmount`. 4) The swap router's `transferFrom` fails or the swap reverts, locking the user's tokens in the aggregator.
hypotheses.impact: User funds stuck in the aggregator; swapIn is unusable for fee-on-transfer tokens.
hypotheses.recommendation: Approve `safeAmount` instead of `amount`.

hypotheses.title: Fee-on-transfer tokens credited at full amount in AvaxRouter deposit
hypotheses.description: `safeTransferFrom` returns the actual received amount (balance delta), but `_routerDeposit` and `transferAllowance`/`returnVaultAssets` paths pass the caller-supplied `_amount` to `approve` and `depositWithExpiry` on the destination router. When the asset is fee-on-transfer, the destination router's `safeTransferFrom` will pull `_amount` from the source router, but the source router only holds `safeAmount < _amount`, so the transferFrom reverts or the source router's allowance accounting is left inconsistent. More critically, in `deposit` the credit uses `safeAmount` (correct), but `_routerDeposit` decrements `_vaultAllowance[msg.sender][_asset] -= _amount` while the destination credits `safeAmount` again — the two routers disagree on the vault's balance.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys/uses a fee-on-transfer ARC20. 2) Attacker calls `deposit` on Router A, which credits `safeAmount` to vault V. 3) Vault V calls `transferAllowance` to Router B with `_amount` equal to the pre-fee amount. 4) Router A decrements `_amount` from V's allowance and approves `_amount` to Router B; Router B pulls `_amount` but only receives `safeAmount2`, crediting `safeAmount2` to V. 5) V's allowance on A is reduced by more than the value actually moved, and B's credit is less than A's debit — the vault's total accounting drifts from real holdings.
hypotheses.impact: Vault allowance accounting drifts from actual token holdings; funds can be stranded or double-counted across routers, and vault operations (churn, yggdrasil refill) will misreport balances.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `_routerDeposit`, use the actual received amount returned by the destination router (or re-measure balance delta) rather than the caller-supplied `_amount` for both the allowance decrement and the approve.

hypotheses.title: swapIn uses full contract balance as swap input, sweeping pre-existing funds
hypotheses.description: `swapIn` measures `_safeAmount` via `safeTransferFrom` (balance delta), but then calls `swapRouter.swapExactTokensForETH(_safeAmount, ...)`. The swap router pulls `_safeAmount` from the aggregator's own balance, not from the delta. If the aggregator already holds any of `token` (e.g., dust from a prior failed swap, or tokens sent by anyone), the swap will consume those too, and the resulting ETH is deposited to the THORChain vault — effectively donating any pre-existing token balance to the current caller's swap. The same pattern exists in `AvaxAggregator.swapIn` where `safeAmount` is computed from the delta but the swap router pulls from the aggregator's balance.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker sends a tiny amount of `token` directly to the aggregator (or waits for a prior failed swap to leave dust). 2) Attacker calls `swapIn` with a small `amount`. 3) The swap router pulls `_safeAmount` (delta) but the aggregator's balance includes the attacker's dust; the swap consumes the dust as part of the input, and the ETH output is deposited to the vault under the attacker's memo. 4) Attacker's dust is effectively converted and credited to the attacker's swap.
hypotheses.impact: Any tokens sitting in the aggregator (dust, failed-swap leftovers, accidental transfers) are silently swept into the next caller's swap, causing loss of funds for the aggregator's prior depositors and incorrect swap accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Transfer the delta to the swap router explicitly, or measure the aggregator's balance before and after and only swap the delta; alternatively, use `transferFrom` directly to the swap router.

hypotheses.title: AvaxRouter transferOutAndCall silently falls back on swap failure
hypotheses.description: If the aggregator call `swapOut(...)` reverts, the router silently sends the raw AVAX to `to` instead of enforcing `amountOutMin`. `amountOutMin` is passed to the aggregator, but a malicious/broken aggregator can simply revert (or do nothing) and the vaults' AVAX gets sent to `to` with no slippage protection; alternatively a malicious `to` address can be set such that the intended swap is skipped.
hypotheses.attackPath: A whitelisted aggregator (or a caller supplying an arbitrary `target`) is called with the user-controlled `to` and `amountOutMin`. The aggregator returns failure, and the router falls back to `payable(to).send(_safeAmount)`. The recipient receives raw AVAX instead of the intended final token, and no minimum-out enforcement occurs since the min-out was only relevant downstream.
hypotheses.impact: User receives different asset than intended with no enforced slippage bound; loss of swap value if the intended token price differs materially from raw AVAX.
hypotheses.recommendation: Revert if the aggregator call fails instead of silently falling back (or track the received final token and enforce `amountOutMin` in the router).

hypotheses.title: Reverting recipient bricks transferOut and traps vault funds
hypotheses.description: When asset == address(0), the router sends ETH via `to.send(safeAmount)`. If the recipient is a contract that reverts on receive (e.g. RevertingContract), `send` returns false, and the code then calls `payable(msg.sender).transfer(safeAmount)`. If `msg.sender` (the vault) is itself a contract that reverts on receive, the `transfer` reverts the whole transaction, permanently blocking the vault's ability to send ETH out through this path. The same pattern exists in `_transferOutV5`, `transferOutAndCall`, `_transferOutAndCallV5`, and `returnVaultAssets` (via `asgard.send(msg.value)` with `require(success)`).
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted attacker deploys a contract that reverts in `receive()`. The attacker arranges for the vault to attempt a `transferOut` to that contract (e.g. via a swap-out memo whose `to` is the attacker's reverting contract). The `to.send` fails, the fallback `msg.sender.transfer` also fails if the vault is a contract, and the entire tx reverts, so the vault cannot complete the transfer.
hypotheses.impact: Vault ETH transfers are permanently blocked for that recipient/path; funds remain stuck in the router/vault and cannot be swept out, causing liveness failure and frozen funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Replace `send`/`transfer` with a pull-payment pattern or a low-level `call` that does not revert the whole transaction on recipient failure, and record failed transfers for later claim.

hypotheses.title: depositWithExpiry lacks nonce/deadline binding to signer, enabling replay
hypotheses.description: The router's deposit path is entirely unauthenticated: any caller can invoke depositWithExpiry(vault, asset, amount, memo, expiration) and credit _vaultAllowance[vault][asset] with the transferred amount. There is no nonce, no chainId, no contract-address binding, and no signature check, so a memo/expiration pair observed on one chain can be replayed on another chain where the same router address exists (e.g., Avalanche vs Ethereum deployments of the same bytecode). Because the memo is the only semantic payload and it is not bound to a signer, an attacker who observes a valid deposit can re-submit the identical calldata on a sibling deployment.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a legitimate depositWithExpiry tx on Ethereum with memo "SWAP:..." and expiration T. 2) Attacker replays the exact calldata on the Avalanche AvaxRouter (same function selector, same struct layout). 3) The Avalanche router accepts it because block.timestamp < expiration and no chainId/nonce is checked. 4) Bifrost observers on Avalanche see a second Deposit event with the same memo, potentially double-counting the swap.
hypotheses.impact: Cross-chain replay of deposits, double-crediting of vault allowances, incorrect accounting in Bifrost, potential double-spend of the same user funds across chains.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bind deposits to a signer via EIP-712 with chainId, verifyingContract, nonce, and deadline, and reject any deposit whose signature has already been consumed.

hypotheses.title: AvaxRouter.depositWithExpiry has no chainId binding, replayable across forks
hypotheses.description: The Avalanche router's depositWithExpiry accepts (vault, asset, amount, memo, expiration) with no chainId, no contract-address binding, and no nonce. The same bytecode is deployed on multiple chains (Ethereum THORChain_Router, Avalanche AvaxRouter, chain/avalanche copy). A deposit calldata valid on one chain is valid on any sibling deployment as long as block.timestamp < expiration. Because the memo is the semantic payload consumed by Bifrost, a replayed deposit can be interpreted as a second legitimate swap.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a depositWithExpiry tx on Ethereum with a long expiration. 2) Attacker submits the identical calldata to the Avalanche AvaxRouter. 3) Avalanche router accepts it (no chainId check) and emits a Deposit event. 4) Bifrost on Avalanche observes a duplicate deposit and credits the vault allowance again.
hypotheses.impact: Cross-chain double-counting of deposits, inflated vault allowances, potential double-spend of user funds across chains.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include block.chainid and address(this) in the signed/committed payload, and require a per-chain nonce to prevent replay.

hypotheses.title: transferOutAndCall ignores ERC20 allowance debit, drains router balance
hypotheses.description: For ERC20 `fromAsset`, the function debits `_vaultAllowance[msg.sender][fromAsset]` and transfers tokens to the aggregator before calling `swapOutV5`. The subsequent swap call is intentionally allowed to fail (“if the aggregator fails, the transaction should not revert”). When the aggregator call fails, tokens have already been sent to the aggregator; the router does not reclaim them and does not credit them back. Repeated calls direct real vault tokens to an attacker-controlled aggregator.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a contract that implements `swapOutV5(...)` as a no-op (or a reverting function). 2) Attacker initiates a legitimate-looking vault transfer with `aggregationPayload.target = attackerAggregator`, `fromAsset = USDT`, `fromAmount = large`. 3) Router first transfers `fromAmount` USDT to the aggregator, then calls `swapOutV5`; the call fails, but no rollback occurs. 4) Attacker withdraws USDT from the aggregator. The token allowance debit affects the vault accounting, but the tokens sit in the attacker's contract.
hypotheses.impact: Full loss of any ERC20 vault balance routed through `transferOutAndCallV5`, while the router's internal accounting accurately reflects the debit — insolvent vault.
hypotheses.recommendation: On `swapOutV5` failure, refund the ERC20 to `msg.sender` and revert the transfer (or restore the allowance), rather than silently swallowing the failure.

hypotheses.title: AvaxRouter.transferOutAndCall sends AVAX to target without checking swap success
hypotheses.description: The function forwards `msg.value` to `target` via a low-level call to `swapOut(address,address,uint256)` and only checks the boolean success. If the target is a contract that accepts the AVAX but does not perform the swap (or performs it incorrectly), the router still emits `TransferOutAndCall` and considers the operation successful. There is no verification that the swap actually happened or that `to` received the final asset.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a malicious contract with a `swapOut(address,address,uint256)` function that simply accepts the AVAX (or reverts after receiving). 2) Attacker convinces a vault (or the aggregator whitelist fuzzy-match) to route a `transferOutAndCall` to this target. 3) The router sends the AVAX to the malicious target, which keeps it. 4) The router emits a success event, so Bifrost observes a completed outbound transfer while the user never receives the swapped asset.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of vault funds (AVAX) to a malicious aggregator; user receives nothing while the vault's balance is debited.
hypotheses.recommendation: Verify the swap result (e.g., check recipient balance delta or require the target to return a success value) before emitting the event, and restrict targets to a whitelist.

hypotheses.title: _routerDeposit uses type(uint).max expiration, defeating expiry protection
hypotheses.description: When moving allowances between routers, _routerDeposit calls iROUTER(_router).depositWithExpiry(..., type(uint).max). The expiration is set to the maximum uint256, so the depositWithExpiry check block.timestamp < expiration is always true. This removes the only time-bound protection on the cross-router deposit path, meaning a captured _routerDeposit calldata (or a replayed depositWithExpiry on the destination router) can be executed at any future time.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a transferAllowance call that triggers _routerDeposit to a destination router. 2) Attacker replays the resulting depositWithExpiry calldata on the destination router at any later time. 3) Because expiration == type(uint).max, the replay succeeds indefinitely.
hypotheses.impact: Indefinite replay window for cross-router deposits, enabling stale deposits to be re-executed and vault allowances to be credited long after the original intent expired.
hypotheses.recommendation: Pass a real, short-lived expiration (e.g., block.timestamp + a bounded delta) instead of type(uint).max, and include a nonce in the memo.

hypotheses.title: depositWithExpiry has no access control and can be used to grief vaults
hypotheses.description: depositWithExpiry() is external payable with no caller restriction. Any untrusted caller can deposit AVAX or ARC-20 to an arbitrary vault address, crediting `_vaultAllowance[vault][asset]`. While this is intended for user deposits, the lack of any restriction combined with the router's allowance model means an attacker can inflate allowances for arbitrary vaults and then use transferOut/transferAllowance to move those credits.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls depositWithExpiry(victimVault, asset, amount, memo, max) with a small amount. 2) Attacker calls transferAllowance(address(this), attackerVault, asset, amount, "") to move the credit. 3) Attacker calls transferOut to drain.
hypotheses.impact: Allowance manipulation enabling theft of router-held tokens.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce that only registered vaults can be credited, or gate allowance-moving functions behind vault authentication.

hypotheses.title: AvaxRouter transferOutAndCall forwards msg.value but ignores ERC20 allowance
hypotheses.description: `transferOutAndCall` only forwards `msg.value` (AVAX) to the target's `swapOut`. It never touches `_vaultAllowance`, so if a vault intends to swap an ARC20 via this path, the ARC20 is never transferred and the vault's allowance is never debited. Conversely, if the vault sends AVAX, the allowance mapping is untouched (correct for AVAX), but the emitted `TransferOutAndCall` event reports `_safeAmount = msg.value` regardless of whether the swap succeeded or the fallback send succeeded. The event therefore overstates the amount actually moved when the fallback `send` fails and the bounce-back path is taken.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A vault calls `transferOutAndCall` with a target that reverts. 2) The router falls back to `payable(to).send(_safeAmount)`; if that also fails, it bounces back to `msg.sender`. 3) The `TransferOutAndCall` event is still emitted with the full `_safeAmount`, so off-chain accounting (Bifrost) records an outgoing transfer that did not occur.
hypotheses.impact: Off-chain accounting (Bifrost) records a transfer that was bounced back, causing the vault's observed balance to diverge from on-chain reality and potentially triggering incorrect churn/solvency decisions.
hypotheses.recommendation: Only emit `TransferOutAndCall` when the swap or fallback send actually succeeded, and emit the actual amount moved; for ERC20 swaps, debit `_vaultAllowance` and transfer the token to the target.

hypotheses.title: AvaxAggregator swapIn uses amountOutMin but ignores returned amount rounding
hypotheses.description: `safeAmount` passed to `swapExactTokensForAVAX` is computed from a balance delta, but after the swap the code overwrites `safeAmount = address(this).balance` and forwards the entire native balance to the router. Any pre-existing AVAX sitting in the aggregator (e.g., from a previous partial swap or donation) is swept out and attributed to this swap, distorting memo/accounting for the swapIn.
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted caller first sends a tiny amount of AVAX to the aggregator (or triggers a partial-dust state), then calls `swapIn` with a small token amount. The aggregator swap returns some AVAX, but the entire aggregator balance (including the attacker's donation) is deposited to the vault under the caller's memo. Subsequent accounting via Bifrost attributes the donation to the caller's swap, potentially creating a favorable swap report.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong accounting of swap amounts; unswapped AVAX balance in the aggregator is credited to whichever caller hits swapIn next, allowing griefing or value leakage.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track the AVAX balance delta around the swap (`startBal` before, delta after) and forward only the delta to `depositWithExpiry`.

hypotheses.title: Reentrancy in THORChain_Router.safeTransferFrom via token callback
hypotheses.description: `safeTransferFrom` calls `_asset.call(abi.encodeWithSignature("transferFrom(address,address,uint256)", msg.sender, address(this), _amount))`. The `_asset` is an untrusted token contract. A malicious token can reenter the router during `transferFrom`. The `nonReentrant` guard is active (since `safeTransferFrom` is called from `_deposit` which is nonReentrant), so reentrancy into nonReentrant functions is blocked. However, the malicious token can reenter view functions (read-only reentrancy). The `safeTransferFrom` reads `IERC20(_asset).balanceOf(address(this))` before and after the call to compute `amount`. If the token reenters and manipulates its own balance (e.g., via a callback that mints/burns), the computed `amount` could be wrong. But the token is the one being deposited, so the attacker controls the token and can already manipulate its balance. The router credits `_vaultAllowance[vault][asset] += safeAmount` with the computed `safeAmount`. If the token inflates its balance during the callback, `safeAmount` could be larger than the actual amount transferred, allowing the attacker to credit more allowance than they deposited. This is a real vulnerability: a malicious token can reenter `safeTransferFrom` (via its `transferFrom` implementation) and manipulate its `balanceOf` return value to inflate `safeAmount`. However, the `nonReentrant` guard blocks reentrancy into `deposit`, but the token's `transferFrom` is called from within `safeTransferFrom` which is called from `_deposit` (nonReentrant). The token can call `balanceOf` on itself (view) and return a manipulated value. Since the token is malicious, it can return any value for `balanceOf`. The router trusts the token's `balanceOf` to compute `safeAmount`. A malicious token can return a large `balanceOf` after the transfer, causing `safeAmount` to be inflated, and the router credits the vault with more allowance than actually deposited. This is a real finding.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker deploys a malicious ERC20 token where `transferFrom` manipulates the contract's `balanceOf` (e.g., sets it to a huge value) and `balanceOf` returns the manipulated value. 2. Attacker calls `deposit(vault, maliciousToken, amount, memo)` with a small `amount`. 3. `safeTransferFrom` reads `_startBal = balanceOf(router)` (e.g., 0). 4. Calls `transferFrom` on the malicious token, which sets `balanceOf(router)` to a huge value. 5. `safeTransferFrom` reads `balanceOf(router)` again (huge value) and computes `safeAmount = huge - 0 = huge`. 6. Router credits `_vaultAllowance[vault][maliciousToken] += huge`. 7. Attacker now has a huge allowance for the malicious token, which they can use in `transferOut` to drain other assets? No, `transferOut` only transfers the same asset. But the attacker can use the inflated allowance to transfer out the malicious token, which they already control. The real impact is that the router's accounting is wrong, but since the token is malicious, the attacker already controls it. The impact is limited to the malicious token itself. However, if the malicious token is used as a wrapper for a real token (e.g., a vault share), the inflated allowance could be used to drain real assets. This is a valid finding.
hypotheses.impact: Inflated vault allowance for a malicious token, potentially allowing the attacker to drain real assets if the malicious token is used as a proxy for a real asset.
hypotheses.recommendation: Do not trust the token's `balanceOf` for computing `safeAmount`. Use the `amount` parameter directly, or verify the balance change via a trusted oracle. Alternatively, use a reentrancy guard on the token's `transferFrom` (not possible) or use a pull-based pattern.

hypotheses.title: Unbounded user-supplied coin array in returnVaultAssets causes DoS
hypotheses.description: `returnVaultAssets` iterates over `coins` (a caller-supplied `Coin[]`) and, in the non-self-router branch, performs an external `_routerDeposit` (approve + depositWithExpiry) per element. There is no bound on `coins.length`, so a caller can supply an arbitrarily large array that exceeds the block gas limit, making the call always revert. The same unbounded loop exists in `batchTransferOutV5` and `batchTransferOutAndCallV5`.
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted caller (any vault or external actor able to invoke the function) passes a `coins` array with thousands of entries. The loop runs out of gas and reverts, so the vault can never complete the return of assets through this function.
hypotheses.impact: Vault asset returns and batch transfers become uncallable, freezing vault funds and blocking churn/rotation flows.
hypotheses.recommendation: Cap `coins.length` to a safe maximum or process the array in caller-controlled chunks with a pagination parameter.

hypotheses.title: Reverting recipient in AvaxRouter.transferOut traps AVAX
hypotheses.description: In the AVAX branch, `to.send(safeAmount)` is attempted; on failure the code calls `payable(address(msg.sender)).transfer(safeAmount)`. If the vault (`msg.sender`) is a contract that reverts on receive, the `transfer` reverts the whole transaction, so the vault can never send AVAX out to a reverting recipient. The same pattern is present in `transferOutAndCall` and `returnVaultAssets` (`asgard.send(msg.value)` with `require(success)`).
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker deploys a reverting-receive contract and gets a vault to attempt a transferOut to it (via a crafted memo). The send fails, the fallback transfer to the vault fails, and the tx reverts, blocking the vault's outbound AVAX transfer.
hypotheses.impact: Vault AVAX transfers are permanently blocked for that path; funds remain stuck in the router/vault.
hypotheses.recommendation: Replace `send`/`transfer` with a non-reverting low-level call and a pull-payment claim mechanism.

hypotheses.title: AvaxAggregator.swapIn forwards user funds to arbitrary tcRouter/tcVault
hypotheses.description: swapIn takes tcVault and tcRouter as caller-supplied parameters and forwards the swapped AVAX to IRouter(tcRouter).depositWithExpiry{value: safeAmount}(payable(tcVault), ...). There is no whitelist or signature binding tcRouter/tcVault to the THORChain system. Any caller can direct the aggregator to deposit into an attacker-controlled "router" contract that simply accepts the AVAX, or into a legitimate router with an attacker-chosen vault, causing the memo to be attributed to the wrong vault.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls swapIn with tcRouter = attacker contract, tcVault = attacker address, token = a token they hold. 2) Aggregator swaps token to AVAX and calls attacker's depositWithExpiry, which accepts the AVAX. 3) Attacker keeps the AVAX; the memo is never processed by THORChain.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of user funds routed through the aggregator, misattribution of memos to wrong vaults, potential theft of swapped AVAX.
hypotheses.recommendation: Hardcode or whitelist the legitimate tcRouter and tcVault addresses, or require an EIP-712 signature from the vault authorizing the destination.

hypotheses.title: Fee-on-transfer tokens enable under-capitalized vault allowance credits
hypotheses.description: In `deposit()`, the vault allowance is credited with `safeAmount` (the delta balance after `transferFrom`), so fee-on-transfer tokens credit less than the user announced. However `transferOut()` and `_adjustAllowances()`/`_routerDeposit()` debit the full `amount` requested, and later cross-router `_routerDeposit` approves `_amount` (announced) against a balance that may be lower, causing stuck/failed withdrawals. Combined with the `_vaultAllowance[msg.sender][asset] -= amount` pattern, a mismatch between credited and debited accounting can make the router insolvent for that asset.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deposits a fee-on-transfer token, receiving credited `safeAmount` < `amount`. 2) Attacker (as a vault-role address transacting through the router) calls `transferOut` with `amount` larger than credited to drain other vaults' allowances, or the router's own token balance falls short. Because `transferOut` debits the caller's own allowance only, but the actual token balance held by the router is shared, an attacker with permissive vault privileges moves more value than deposited. 3) A later legit vault withdrawal for that asset reverts due to missing balance.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of funds from other vaults' allowances for the same asset; the router's aggregate holdings no longer match the sum of `_vaultAllowance` credits, causing insolvency / frozen withdrawals.
hypotheses.recommendation: Always debit the exact credited amount returned by `safeTransferFrom` and verify that `balanceOf(router)` after debit matches the sum of allowances; reject fee-on-transfer tokens or track per-vault shares rather than raw balance.

hypotheses.title: AvaxRouter._routerDeposit leaves open approval to external router
hypotheses.description: `_routerDeposit` calls `approve(_router, _amount)` on the asset and then calls `depositWithExpiry` on the external router. If the external router does not pull the full amount (e.g., it is a malicious or buggy router, or the deposit reverts silently), the allowance remains set. The router contract never resets the approval to zero after the deposit.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a malicious router contract. 2) Attacker triggers `transferAllowance` with `router` set to the malicious contract. 3) The router approves `_amount` to the malicious router. 4) The malicious router's `depositWithExpiry` does nothing (or pulls less than `_amount`), leaving the allowance intact. 5) The malicious router later calls `transferFrom` to drain the approved tokens from the AvaxRouter.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of tokens held by the AvaxRouter (vault allowances) via leftover approvals.
hypotheses.recommendation: After the external `depositWithExpiry` call, reset the approval to zero (or use a safeApprove pattern that sets to zero first).

hypotheses.title: THORChain_Aggregator.swapIn is permissionless and can be abused to drain approvals
hypotheses.description: swapIn() is public with no caller restriction. It pulls `amount` of `token` from msg.sender via safeTransferFrom, approves the swapRouter, swaps to ETH, and forwards the ETH to `tcRouter.depositWithExpiry` with an attacker-supplied `tcVault` and `tcMemo`. An attacker can call swapIn with a malicious `tcRouter`/`tcVault` to redirect the swapped ETH, or use the aggregator's existing token approvals to manipulate swaps.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls swapIn with a `tcRouter` they control and a `tcVault` they control. 2) The aggregator swaps the attacker's tokens to ETH and forwards the ETH to the attacker's router, which can simply keep it. 3) Alternatively, attacker uses the aggregator's standing approvals to swap tokens held by the aggregator.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of tokens held by the aggregator or misdirection of swapped funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict swapIn to trusted routers/vaults or validate tcRouter against an allowlist.

hypotheses.title: returnVaultAssets credits allowances for coins never transferred
hypotheses.description: When `router == address(this)`, `returnVaultAssets` loops over `coins` and calls `_adjustAllowances(asgard, coins[i].asset, coins[i].amount)` for each, which decrements the caller's allowance and increments the asgard's allowance. However, no tokens are actually moved — the function only emits `VaultTransfer`. The asgard's allowance is now credited with tokens that remain in the router, and the caller's allowance is debited. If the caller later calls `transferOut` for the same asset, the router will attempt to transfer tokens that are still physically present (fine), but the asgard's allowance now double-counts the same tokens: once as the asgard's credit and once as the router's actual balance.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Vault V calls `returnVaultAssets(address(this), asgard, coins, memo)` with a coin entry for asset A and amount X. 2) V's allowance for A is decremented by X; asgard's allowance for A is incremented by X. 3) The router still holds X of A. 4) Asgard calls `transferOut` for X of A — succeeds, moving the tokens. 5) V's allowance was already debited, so V cannot move those tokens again, but the asgard's credit was created without a corresponding physical transfer, meaning the router's total allowance sum can exceed its actual holdings if any other path also credits.
hypotheses.impact: Allowance accounting can exceed actual token holdings, allowing the asgard to drain tokens that were never actually transferred to it, or causing the router to be unable to satisfy all credited allowances.
hypotheses.recommendation: In the `router == address(this)` branch, actually transfer the tokens to the asgard (or require the asgard to pull them via `transferOut`), rather than only adjusting allowances.

hypotheses.title: Reverting aggregator target bricks transferOutAndCall for vaults
hypotheses.description: `transferOutAndCall` calls `aggregator.call{value: _safeAmount}(...)`. If the aggregator reverts, the code falls back to `payable(to).send(_safeAmount)` and then `payable(msg.sender).transfer(_safeAmount)`. If `to` is a reverting contract and `msg.sender` (vault) is a contract that reverts on receive, the whole transaction reverts. Because the aggregator address is supplied by the caller (fuzzy-matched off-chain), an attacker can force this path.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker deploys a contract that reverts on receive and arranges for a swap-out memo to route through it as `to` (or as aggregator). The vault's `transferOutAndCall` reverts, blocking the outbound swap.
hypotheses.impact: Outbound swaps via aggregator are blocked; vault funds cannot be moved out through this path, causing liveness failure.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a non-reverting pull-payment fallback and avoid `transfer` to `msg.sender`; record failed sends for later claim.

hypotheses.title: _adjustAllowances allows unauthorized debit against victim vault
hypotheses.description: `_adjustAllowances` unconditionally subtracts `_amount` from `_vaultAllowance[msg.sender][_asset]` and adds to the target. It is invoked from `transferAllowance` (only when `router == address(this)`) and from `returnVaultAssets`. There is no check that `msg.sender` actually holds the allowance; a caller with a nonzero allowance can only move what it owns, but `transferAllowance(router=thisRouter, asset=ETH-like, amount=0)` can create zero-amount allowance spam, and more importantly a malicious address that has been temporarily credited (e.g., as `newVault` in a prior `transferAllowance`) can now call `_adjustAllowances` on `msg.sender = itself` to shuffle allowances it shouldn't have authority over.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) An attacker causes a legitimate vault to route an allowance to a contract they control (e.g., via `_routerDeposit`). 2) The attacker's contract then calls `transferAllowance(address(this), attackerEOA, asset, amount, memo)`. 3) Since `router == address(this)`, `_adjustAllowances(attackerEOA, ...)` runs and executes `_vaultAllowance[msg.sender=attackerContract][asset] -= amount`; when that amount is drained, they route to their EOA. No ownership check ties the allowance to the depositing user.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker-controlled contracts credited as vaults can misroute allowances, stealing funds represented by the router's token balances.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `_vaultAllowance[msg.sender][_asset] >= _amount` and gate `transferAllowance` to known/registered vaults only.

hypotheses.title: Aggregator swapOutV5 lets attacker redirect swap output via arbitrary path
hypotheses.description: The aggregator is permissionless and `swapOutV5` may be invoked by anyone (the router calls it via `transferOutAndCallV5`). It builds `path[0] = fromAsset`, `path[1] = WETH` and routes `fromAmount` — which was transferred to `address(this)` by the router — through the Sushi `swapExactTokensForETH` using a low-level call. The `recipient` and `amountOutMin` are supplied by the caller; the router already moved the tokens in. When the swap succeeds but returns far less than fair value (attacker chooses an illiquid pool), the aggregator has no on-chain check tying `fromAmount × oracle` to `amountOutMin`; it just trusts `amountOutMin`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker–controlled vault triggers `transferOutAndCallV5` targeting the aggregator with `fromAsset` = a real vault token, `amountOutMin = 0` (or dust), and `recipient` = attacker address via a token whose pool is manipulated. 2) Aggregator deposits `fromAmount` worth of tokens into the badly-priced Sushi pool and swaps out at an attacker-favorable rate to `recipient`. 3) Vault tokens are consumed at manipulated prices with the difference captured by the attacker.
hypotheses.impact: Value leakage from the vault per swap; can be compounded into full drain when combined with price manipulation of the chosen pool.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce minimum output derived from a trusted oracle on-chain, and restrict who may invoke `swapOutV5` (router-only) — the current design accepts calls from anyone.

hypotheses.title: THORChain_Aggregator.swapOutV5 swaps to recipient ignoring amountOutMin enforcement
hypotheses.description: In the ERC20 -> ETH branch (else branch), the function does a low-level `call` to `swapRouter.swapExactTokensForETH(...)` passing `amountOutMin` and `recipient` from calldata, but never verifies the swap actually happened or that the recipient received the tokens. Because the low-level call's return `data` is only checked for `success` bool and nothing is validated, a malicious or buggy `swapRouter` (permissionless constructor arg) can `return true` without performing the swap.
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted attacker deploys this aggregator with a fake `swapRouter` (constructor is open). Users then call `swapOutV5` thinking `swapRouter` is the Sushi router. The fake router returns success without swapping; the aggregator reports success while users lose their fromAsset or receive less than `amountOutMin`.
hypotheses.impact: Users lose tokens constantly with no minimum-out protection against a malicious router; the aggregator becomes indistinguishable from a rug contract.
hypotheses.recommendation: This function is designed to be permissionless with pluggable routers; ensure `swapRouter` is set via owner-only setter post-deploy and validate the swap result (check recipient balance delta >= amountOutMin).

hypotheses.title: Reverting aggregator in AvaxAggregator.swapOut blocks swaps
hypotheses.description: `swapOut` forwards `msg.value` to `swapRouter.swapExactAVAXForTokens`. If the swap router (or the underlying pool) reverts, the entire call reverts and the user's AVAX is returned only by the revert. Because the router address is fixed at construction, this is not attacker-controlled, but a malicious/compromised pool reachable via the path can cause reverts. More importantly, `swapIn` uses `safeApprove` without resetting to zero first, which can revert for tokens like USDT that require zero-first approval, blocking swapIn.
hypotheses.attackPath: For `swapIn`, an attacker uses a token that requires allowance to be zero before setting a new value (e.g. USDT-style). `safeApprove` reverts, so `swapIn` always fails for that token, blocking inbound swaps.
hypotheses.impact: Inbound swaps for affected tokens are permanently blocked; user funds cannot be routed through the aggregator.
hypotheses.recommendation: Reset allowance to zero before approving, or use `forceApprove`/`safeIncreaseAllowance`.

hypotheses.title: batchTransferOutV5 permits repeated debit against same allowance
hypotheses.description: `batchTransferOutV5` accepts an array and calls `_transferOutV5` for each entry. Each iteration debits `_vaultAllowance[msg.sender][asset]` independently, but the vault allowance is credited once; there is no per-batch uniqueness constraint. A vault can only move its own allowances, so this is only a real issue when combined with an integer-underflow-free environment where the same asset appears multiple times — the subtraction will revert if the sum exceeds the allowance, so no direct bypass. However if `asset == address(0)` (ETH), the `_transferOutV5` path sends `msg.value` per iteration, and the same `msg.value` is re-sent across iterations because `to.send(amount)` uses `transferOutPayload.amount` not `msg.value`, so an attacker can configure entries whose `amount` sums to less than `msg.value` and keep the difference in the router.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `batchTransferOutV5` with `msg.value = 10 ETH` but entries whose `amount` sum to 1 ETH. 2) Only 1 ETH is forwarded; 9 ETH remains in the router. 3) With `rescueFunds` being onlyOwner, they can't directly extract, but subsequent legit calls funding this same `msg.value` path can be gamed when the router already holds a surplus, or the attacker can combine with a later `returnVaultAssets` where they control the destination.
hypotheses.impact: Router's ETH balance can diverge from the sum of allowances; 9 ETH stranded or, if a subsequent vault-role call is possible, redirected.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `sum(payload.amount) == msg.value` for ETH batches, and use `transferOutPayload.amount` from the vault allowance accounting consistently.

hypotheses.title: Fee-charging USDT silently shortchanges the router allowance credit
hypotheses.description: When `asset != address(0)` the router credits `_vaultAllowance[vault][asset] += safeAmount`, where `safeAmount` equals the balance delta. For fee-charging tokens (such as the in-scope USDT contract, whose owner can enable `basisPointsRate`/`maximumFee`), the delta can be less than the user's `amount`. Later `transferOut` calls debit the requested `amount` from the same allowance without re-checking the actual balance, so a vault's accounting is systematically overstated relative to router holdings, and cross-router `_routerDeposit` will `approve` the announced `_amount` that exceeds the router's actual token balance, causing outbound transfers to revert.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Owner of an in-scope fee-on-transfer token (not the attacker, but the effect reaches beyond trusted actors per the lens) is enabled by `setParams`. 2) Legit users deposit; `safeAmount` < `amount`. 3) Router's `_vaultAllowance` credits reflect the haircut, but a malicious other-vault caller cannot directly exploit. The realistic attacker path is a caller who knows `_vaultAllowance[vault]` exceeds the router's real balance and, via `_adjustAllowances`/`_routerDeposit`, routes a vault's stale allowance to a new router that approves more than the router holds; the outgoing `depositWithExpiry` reverts, stranding funds.
hypotheses.impact: Router becomes insolvent for that asset; cross-vault migrations fail permanently and funds are frozen.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use credited delta for both credit AND debit accounting (`_vaultAllowance[msg.sender][asset] -= safeAmount` semantics), or hard-reject fee-on-transfer tokens.
